```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(238)
mytheme <- theme(
  title = element_text(size = 26),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 24),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 26)
)
cmap <- palette.colors(9, "Accent")
speed_of_light <- morley |> pull(Speed)
```

## Example: Speed of light (continued) {.center}

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column}

```{r}
# speed of light
b <- (24 * sqrt(pi))^(1/3) * sd(speed_of_light) * length(speed_of_light)^(-1/3)
ggplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(x = speed_of_light, y = after_stat(density)),
    binwidth = round(b)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Speed of light - 299 000 (km/s)",
       y = "Density") +
  mytheme
```

::::::
:::::: {.column}

+    We modeled the measured speed of light as ________________ realizations from
an ______________ distribution.
+    That is, we modeled them as realizations of a **random sample**.

::::::
:::::::

## Is the speed of light data set a random sample? {.center}

:::::::: {.columns}
::::::: {.column width="45%"}

Do they follow the same distribution?

:::::::
::::::: {.column width="10%"}
:::::::
::::::: {.column width="45%"}

Are the observations independent?

:::::::
::::::::

:::::::: {.columns}
::::::: {.column width="45%"}

+  The measurements were collected under the same experimental conditions.

+  They were estimates for a one "true" value.

:::::::
::::::: {.column width="10%"}
:::::::
::::::: {.column width="45%"}

+  Physical independence -- the events associated with experiments have no
physical connections -- implies stochastic independence.

+  When collecting the speed of light data, Michelson ensured the measurements
had no influence to each other.

:::::::
::::::::

## Statistical model for repeated measurements (univariate) {.half-title .center}

:::: {.column width="45%"}

+  The probability distribution $F$ is the **statistical model**.
+  We assume that there exists one _true distribution_.<sup>&#8224;</sup>

::: {.in-column-footer}

<sup>&#8224;</sup>At least until we talk about Bayesian estimation.

:::

::::


::::: {.full-height .right}

<br />

::: {.definition}

A data set consisting of repeated measurements $x_1$, $x_2$, ..., $x_n$ 
of the same quantity is modelled as the realization of a random sample
$X_1$, $X_2$, ..., $X_n$.

The model may include a partial specification of the probability
distribution of each $X_i$.
:::

:::::

## Example: A statistical model for the speed of light measurements

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column}

### What we know/believe ...

+  The speed of light in a vacuum is constant.
+  The observed randomness is due to measurement errors.
+  The experiment was carefully designed to avoid any systematic error.
+  The error is likely to be of a large magnitude.

::::::
:::::: {.column}

### How we may model our knowledge/belief ...

+  The observed values are centred around the speed of light in a vacuum.
+  The expectation of the error is 0.
+  The errors have a finite variance.
+  The distribution of the error is symmetric around 0 and tapers off in both
ways.

::::::
:::::::

::: {.text-center .note}
We can model $\text{Measurement}=\text{True speed}+\text{Error}$,
which implies that  
$\mathbb{E}(\text{Measurement})=\text{True speed}$
and $\text{Var}(\text{Measurement})=\text{Var}(\text{Error})<\infty$.
:::

## Example: The true speed of light 

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column}

```{r}
# speed of light
ggplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(x = speed_of_light, y = after_stat(density)),
    binwidth = round(b), fill = "lightgrey"
  ) +
```
```{r}
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 800, sd = 100),
                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 900, sd = 120),
                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 850, sd = 50),
                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 840, sd = 75),
                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  labs(x = "Speed of light - 299 000 (km/s)",
       y = "Density") +
  mytheme
```


::::::
:::::: {.column}

### We _partially_ specified the model by now.


+  We started from $X_i\sim F_i$.
+  We assumed _____________________, $X_1,X_2,\ldots, X_n\sim F$
+  We now assumed $X_1,X_2,\ldots, X_n\sim N(c + 0, \sigma^2)$, where $c$ is the
true speed of light.


::::::
:::::::

::::::: {.columns}

```{r}

ggplot() +

  geom_histogram(
    aes(x = speed_of_light, y = after_stat(density)),
    binwidth = round(b), fill = "lightgrey"
  ) +

                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 900, sd = 120),
                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 850, sd = 50),
                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  geom_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 840, sd = 75),
                alpha = .8, color = "magenta") +
  labs(x = "Speed of light - 299 000 (km/s)",
       y = "Density") +
  mytheme
```


::::::
:::::: {.column}

### We _partially_ specified the model by now.

+    The model suggests a family of distributions as candidates for the true distribution.
+    Specifying the **model parameter(s)**, $\theta$ fully specifies the model.
    +    In this case, $\theta=(c, \sigma^2)$.
+    The partially spcified model is called a **parametric model**.

$$\left\{F_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\right\}$$

## Sample statistic {.half-title .center}

::::: {.column width="45%"}

+  With a model adequately representing the data, sample statistics reflect
features of the distribution.

+  Note that a sample statistic is a random variable.

:::::

::::: {.full-height .right}

<br />

::: {.definition}

Consider a random sample $X_1$, $X_2$, ..., $X_n$. 
A **sample statistic** is a function of the random sample,

$$h(X_1, X_2,\ldots,X_n).$$

:::
:::::

## The Weak Law of Large Numbers

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column}
::: {.definition}

Consider a sequence of independent random variables $X_1$, $X_2$, ...,
with each having the same mean $\mu<\infty$ and the same variance 
$\sigma^2<\infty$. Then for all $\varepsilon>0$,

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}P(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)=0,$$
where $\bar{X}_n=\left.\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right/n$. In other words,

$$\bar{X}_n\overset{p}{\rightarrow}\mu\quad\text{as}\quad n\rightarrow\infty.$$

:::
::::::
:::::: {.column}

_Proof:_


::::::
::::::: 

## The Weak Law of Large Numbers

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column}
::: {.definition}

Consider a sequence of independent random variables $X_1$, $X_2$, ...,
with each having the same mean $\mu<\infty$ and the same variance 
$\sigma^2<\infty$. Then for all $\varepsilon>0$,

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}P(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)=0,$$
where $\bar{X}_n=\left.\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right/n$. In other words,

$$\bar{X}_n\overset{p}{\rightarrow}\mu\quad\text{as}\quad n\rightarrow\infty.$$

:::
::::::
:::::: {.column}

_Proof:_

::: {.note}

Recall Chebyshevy's inequality states that

$$P(|Y-\mathbb{E}(Y)|\ge \varepsilon)\le\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\text{Var}(Y).$$

for a random variable $Y$ with $\mathbb{E}(Y)<\infty$
and $\text{Var}(Y)<\infty$, and any constant $\varepsilon>0$.

:::

::::::
::::::: 

## The Weak Law of Large Numbers

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column}
::: {.definition}

Consider a sequence of independent random variables $X_1$, $X_2$, ...,
with each having the same mean $\mu<\infty$ and the same variance 
$\sigma^2<\infty$. Then for all $\varepsilon>0$,

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}P(|\bar{X}_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)=0,$$
where $\bar{X}_n=\left.\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right/n$. In other words,

$$\bar{X}_n\overset{p}{\rightarrow}\mu\quad\text{as}\quad n\rightarrow\infty.$$

:::
::::::
:::::: {.column}

+  A random sample is a sequence of independent and identically distributed 
random variables.

+  The **sample mean** of a random sample estimates the expectation 
of the model distribution.

+  The sample mean is an example of a **sample statistic**.

::::::
:::::::

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column}

```{r}
# speed of light
ggplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(x = speed_of_light, y = after_stat(density)),
    binwidth = round(b), fill = "lightgrey"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(speed_of_light), color = cmap[1], linewidth = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 792.458, color = cmap[3], linewidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "Speed of light - 299 000 (km/s)",
       y = "Density") +
  mytheme
```


::::::
:::::: {.column}

::: {.r-fit-text}

The **sample mean** is a good candidate as the estimate.

:::


+  `r format(round(299000 + mean(speed_of_light)), big.mark = " ")` km/s is the <span class="accent-one">sample mean</span> of the observations.
+  299\ 792 km/s is the <span class="accent-three">actual</span> speed of light in vacuum.

::: {.note}

After adjusting for bending of light in the air, Michelson first estimated 299\ 940 km/s (1882) then improved the adjustment method to estimate 299\ 796 km/s.

:::

::: {.note}

Actually, the meter is defined as the length of the path light travels in vacuum in ${\frac{1}{299\ 792\ 458}}$ of a second.

:::

## Example: Variance of speed of light measurements

:::::::: {.columns}
::::::: {.column}

The speed of light in a vacuum is now defined as exactly
299 792.458 km/s. 

Let $X_i\overset{i.i.d}{\sim}F_{\theta}$ for
$i=1,\ldots,n$ represent speed of light measurements in km/s
where $\theta=(\mu, \sigma^2)$.
$\mu=299\ 792.458$ is the mean and $\sigma^2$ is the unknown variance
of the measurements.


:::::::
::::::: {.column}


Suppose we estimate the true variance $\sigma^2$ with

$$\widetilde{s}_n^2=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i-\mu)^2.$$

Show that $\widetilde{s}_n^2\overset{p}{\to}\sigma^2$. 

What extra conditions are required on $X_i$?


:::::::
::::::::

## Example: Variance of speed of light measurements

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column}

::: {.note}

$X_i$'s are i.i.d random variables.

$\implies (X_i-\mu)^2$  are i.i.d r.v.s.

$\implies\widetilde{s}_n^2$ is a sample mean.

:::
::::
:::: {.column}

::: {.note}
Required conditions for the LLN:

1.  $\mathbb{E}\left[\left(X_i-\mu\right)^2\right]=\sigma^2<\infty$
2.  $\text{Var}\left[\left(X_i-\mu\right)^2\right]<\infty$

:::
::::
:::::

<hr />

Then, $\widetilde{s}_n^2$ converges in probability to the mean of $(X_1-\mu)^2$.

$$\begin{split}
& \mathbb{E}\left[\left(X_1-\mu\right)^2\right]\\
=& \mathbb{E}\left[X_1^2-2\mu X_1+\mu^2\right] \\
=& \mathbb{E}\left[X_1^2\right]-2\mu \mathbb{E}\left[X_1\right]+\mu^2 \\
=& \mathbb{E}\left[X_1^2\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[X_1\right] & (\mathbb{E}(X_1)=\mu) \\
=& \text{Var}(X_1) & (\text{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}(X^2) - \left[\mathbb{E}(X)\right]^2\text{ for any r.v. }X)\\
=& \sigma^2
\end{split}$$
    
$$\implies\widetilde{s}_n^2\overset{p}{\to}\sigma^2$$

## Example: Estimating probabilities via simulation

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column}

<b class="accent-three">ECDF</b> 50 simulated values vs. 
<b class="accent-five">CDF</b> of Exp(1)

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: .8

set.seed(3264)
sim <- rexp(50, 1)

ggplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = c(0.5, 0.5), xend = c(0.5, 0),
    y = c(0, mean(sim < .5)), yend = c(mean(sim < .5), mean(sim < .5)),
    linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  geom_function(fun = pexp, colour = cmap[5], linewidth = 1.5, alpha = .7) +
  geom_step(aes(x = sim), stat = "ecdf", colour = cmap[3], linewidth = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, mean(sim < .5), 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  mytheme

```

::::
:::: {.column}

```{r eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
sim <- rexp(50)
```



+  Sample proportion of values less than any value $x$ is a sample mean of
$$\mathbb{1}_{\{X_i< x\}}$$

+  The sample proportion converges to the probability that the population random 
variable is less than $x$.

```{r echo=TRUE}
pexp(0.5)
```

+  WLLN justifies using ECDF as an approximation of the CDF.


::::
:::::


## Example: Estimating probabilities via simulation

::::: {.columns}

<b class="accent-three">Density histogram</b> 50 simulated values vs.

::::
:::: {.column}

```{r eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
sim <- rexp(50)
```

+  We can, of course, use the sample mean of simulated values to estimate the 
population mean.

```{r echo=TRUE}
mean(sim) 
```

+  WLLN justifies such approximations, especially, as you increase the sample size.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
mean(rexp(100))
```

```{r}
  geom_histogram(aes(x = sim, y = after_stat(density)), fill = cmap[3], bins = 30) +
  geom_function(fun = dexp, colour = cmap[5], linewidth = 1.5, alpha = .7) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(sim)), linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = mean(sim), labels = round(mean(sim), 3)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  mytheme

```

::::
:::: {.column}

```{r eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
sim <- rexp(1000)
```

+  WLLN justifies such approximations, especially, as you increase the sample size.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
mean(sim)
```

# Summary {.half-title .center}

::::: {.full-height .right .incremental}

+  **Statistical models** describe observed data as realizations of
unknown data-generating processes using probability distributions.

+  With prior knowledge about the process, we can assumptions to build choose 
a probability distribution and partially specify a model.

+  The law of large numbers allows us to estimate features of model 
distributions using sample statistics.
